Disclosed EIN dyads: substitutable pairs and merely related ones

Source: R/dyads.R
pf_dyads.Rd

A grant reported to EAGLE RANCH may have been paid to EAGLE RANCH FOUNDATION, and nothing in the name or the address decides which. The cascade cannot resolve that and should not pretend to. This module builds the table that lets it stop trying: one row per disclosed pair of EINs, drawn from Schedule A Part I line 12g and Schedule R Part II.

Dyads, not clusters — the one design decision that matters

The obvious implementation is a transitive closure with a cluster_id per component. Measured on the pooled 2009-2024 disclosures (566,653 pairs over 174,496 EINs), that produces a single component holding 66,973 EINs across 56 states — 38% of every EIN in the graph — chaining The Reinvestment Fund to the Jewish Community Federation of San Francisco to Glacial Ridge Hospital Foundation. A match "verified" against a set that large is unfalsifiable.

A same-city gate does not fix it: the largest same-city component is 407 EINs in Phoenix, merging Florence Crittenton Services of Arizona, the Arizona Medical Association Foundation and Arizona's Children Association.

So this module emits direct edges only. Two EINs are in a dyad when one filing names the other, and never because a third party names them both. pf_dyad_collapse() enforces that by resolving groups only within the candidates of a single grant. See dev/CLUSTER-FINDINGS.md §2.

Substitutable versus related

A Schedule R Part II edge means related, which is much weaker than interchangeable. It links Mayo Clinic Health System-Fairmont to Mayo Clinic Health System-Lake City — two different hospitals — and PLANNED PARENTHOOD GLOBAL to PLANNED PARENTHOOD ACTION FUND, which is a 501(c)(4) and cannot receive the same grant. Relaxing an error definition across those edges launders real errors into passes.

dyad_class therefore separates two things:

substitutable

The arm exists to fund this one body, or carries its name. Three conditions, all measured: see Why exclusivity is the test.

related

Every other disclosed edge. Useful for context and for flagging, never for relaxing a correctness test.

Why exclusivity is the test

A first build classed every Schedule A edge as substitutable and produced an EIN with 905 substitutable partners: the YMCA Retirement Fund, a 509(a)(3) that supports 907 local YMCAs. SparkJoy Foundation supports 408 unrelated Maine charities, Vitalyst Health Foundation 406, Ascension Health 253. A grant reported to Bangor YMCA is not interchangeable with the retirement fund, so a bare Schedule A edge cannot license substitution — 43% of Schedule A edges come from a supporter with more than ten supportees.

The mirror-image failure is the federated sibling: an identical name core catches 337 chapters of ALPHA LAMBDA DELTA, 214 South Carolina Masonic lodges, and 150-odd VOLUNTEERS OF AMERICA affiliates. Siblings are not substitutes either — that is pf_group_siblings() territory, and a warning rather than an invitation to merge.

Both failures are the same measurement: degree. A body with an arm has one to three of them; anything with fifty is a network. So substitutable requires all three of

  1. a Schedule A edge whose supporter names at most max_fanout organisations, or an identical name core in the same state;

  2. both parties sharing a subsection code — a 501(c)(3) and a 501(c)(4) are not substitutes for a private foundation's grant, whatever Schedule R says about them being related;

  3. neither party exceeding max_degree substitutable partners once the first two conditions are applied.

At the defaults this yields 29,238 substitutable pairs with a maximum degree of 5 and no EIN above it, against 129,645 pairs and a maximum of 905 for the naive rule, while retaining 89% of its reach into the MAYBE tier (1,055 of 1,183 top-two pairs on the 50k run). The sweep is dev/sweep-dyad-rules.R; the adjudicated 100 does not discriminate between any of the six rules tried, so this is chosen on graph safety, not on labels.

What it is worth

On a 50,000-grant run, 14.9% of MAYBE grants have a directly disclosed top two, rising to 24.4% inside the tie band, and collapsing dissolves the tie entirely for 1,224 grants (22.2% of the MAYBE tie band). Where the edge fires it is precise: 98.9% of linked top-two pairs share a content token and 54% share an identical name core. Its increment over the disclosure-free name rule in pf_cluster_arms() is 5.0% of the MAYBE tier — this is a direction-and-confirmation feature, not a recall feature.

Pooling fifteen years buys almost nothing over a single year (49% to 52% of known arm pairs) because the ceiling is non-filing, not vintage. Pool for the n_years stability signal, not for coverage.
